newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica reserve bank announce $1.5 bln credit deal.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica reserve bank announce $1.5 bln credit deal.

text.p: South African Reserve Bank governor Chris Stals said on Thursday the central bank had completed the first phase of talks on establishing a syndicated $1.5 billion medium-term credit facility.
Stals said in a statement 12 banks were arranging the facility.
"These credit facilities are utilised from time to time to supplement the country's foreign reserves," he said.

Stals said the new facility had the advantage of covering a longer maturity than normal credit lines, would be negotiated at lower average cost and have greater transparency in the global financial markets.
"It should inspire more confidence in South Africa's ability to provide liquidity when and if needed by the South African foreign exchange market," he added.

"The Reserve Bank is confident that, taking account of the current level of the official foreign reserves and the total of unutilised foreign credit facilities available to the bank, any additional demands for foreign currency that may arise from the further relaxation of exchange controls and not covered by a continued inflow of foreign capital, will be met."
Interest on the three-year $1.5 billion credit facility would be at LIBOR plus 30 basis points.
Twelve banks were acting as arrangers. The commitment fee would be 15 basis points per annum and fees to arrangers would be 20 basis points at $100 million.
The second phase of the deal, to include co-arrangers and lead managers would begin on June 24.
Co-arrangers would receive a fee of 17.5 basis points at $50 million and lead managers at 15 basis points at $25 million, the statement said.
Stals said that at the end of last month, the aggregate of South Africa's foreign credit facilities amounted to the equivalent of 18.5 billion rand, of which only 1.8 billion rand was used.

"After completion (of the new facility), the total credit facilities available to the Reserve Bank may increase, but not to a significant proportion of the new facility, as some existing credit lines will be absorbed within the new facility, or will be terminated on maturity," Stals said.

South Africa's official reserves of gold and foreign exchange surged 51 percent to a record high of 21.8 billion rand in May, boosted by inflows from the partial privatisation of telecommunications utility Telkom.

The Bank said early this month provisional reserves at the end of May stood at 21.8 billion rand, compared to 14.4 billion rand in April, despite the repayment of 700 million rand in foreign credit lines.
In dollar terms, reserves stood at $4.9 billion against the previous peak of just under $4.3 billion in December 1995.

The central bank's move comes amid worries over the size of possible capital outflows when South Africa partially lifts exchange controls on July 1, allowing residents to invest offshore for the first time.
